LPZ-2 (5.9-4.47 cal ka BP): dry; Chenopodiaceae dominate, Artemisia rises; open steppe/desert-steppe.

Pollen from the Early Neolithic (Elshanka) layer, dated by shells to 8000-7900 14C BP (Vybornov's reading, about -7000; shell dates may be too old, and Courel et al. 2021 put Elshanka pottery mostly after -6000): wormwood and Chenopodiaceae 68%, woody pollen about 15% from trees in the river valley; saiga bones here and at Lebyazhinka IV. Vybornov: 'steppe landscapes of southern type spread up to the basin of the River Sok'.

Bottom of the Early Neolithic (Elshanka) layer, dated 8020+/-90 BP on bone (Le-2343, 7038-6718 BC) and 7930+/-90 BP on pottery temper (Ki-14568): 'almost bare of trees', birch rare, herbs with Chenopodiaceae and wormwood predominant (after Morgunova 1995); 'southern steppe and even semi-desert conditions' at the start of the Atlantic. Courel et al. 2021 would date the pottery after -6000.

Preboreal (10.2-9.0 ka BP in the synthesis' table, after Blagoveshchenskaya 2009 and Kremenetski et al. on the Buzuluk pine forest): dry, cool; cold steppes with patches of pine forest. Ages read as 14C (Khotinsky scheme); on either reading the slice is steppe-dominated.
Preboreal: cold steppes with patches of pine forest.
Preboreal to early Boreal: steppe with patches of pine and pine-birch forest.
Boreal (9.0-8.0 ka BP): steppe and forest-steppe with patches of pine and pine-birch forest; forest area probably smaller than steppe.
Late Boreal: true forest-steppe forms in the east of the Volga Upland; pine and pine-birch forests on slopes and interfluves, broadleaf trees absent or single.
Early Atlantic (from 8.0 ka BP): forest-steppe (pine, pine-birch, pine-oak and broadleaf woods) and steppe; birch spreads, first lime, elm, oak and hazel.
Atlantic: forest-steppe and steppe; steppe on south-facing slopes and the low plateau.
Atlantic: forest-steppe with pine-broadleaf woods; forests advancing.
Late Atlantic, the warmest and wettest phase: forests (oak, lime, maple, elm, pine) dominate the central Volga Upland, forest-steppe in its south; steppe patches remain.
Atlantic-Subboreal boundary: the greatest forest cover of the Holocene, here and in the Trans-Volga (Buzuluk).
Early Subboreal: pine-birch and pine-birch-broadleaf forests; broadleaf trees at their widest but beginning to decline.

Early Subboreal (from 4.5 ka BP): forest-steppe with pine-birch-broadleaf woods, broadleaf trees still widespread; the forest maximum lasts to the end of the early Subboreal (Blagoveshchenskaya 2009).

Slice about 10950 cal BP (22 AMS dates, cal BP; Holocene from 10,900-11,000 cal BP): Corylus, Tilia, Ulmus and Quercus arrive, but 'Poaceae and Artemisia remained equally important ... implying the survival of temperate grasslands in a temperate open parkland setting', described as 'deciduous woodlands studded by alkaline grasslands' (full text; qualitative, no AP % in the text). A large basin (about 60 km2) on the Danube floodplain, so the signal is regional.

Pollen zone Z1a (base of a ~9000-yr fen-peat record on the loess/marl lowland, about 500 mm rain at nearby Doksany; zone called Boreal by the authors, base not directly dated, slice approximate): Pinus 30-80%, Juniperus at its maximum, Artemisia and grasses dominate the herbs, frequent fires. Authors: 'a mosaic of sparse pine woods and open areas with abundant grasses, birch, juniper and hazel'. Read in the Czech companion paper (Zprávy ČBS 50); English version Holocene 25:716, doi 10.1177/0959683614566218.

Pollen zone Z1b (mid-Holocene before the Neolithic; upper boundary dated 7236-6952 cal BP at 648 cm): tree pollen 95% of the sum (the record maximum) but 40-60% of it Pinus and Betula, heavy pollen producers; Artemisia continuous, Pulsatilla, Helianthemum, Chenopodiaceae present. Authors read it as forest-steppe: shady forest patches, light birch-pine open woodland (which 'probably prevailed') and open wet, meadow and steppe enclaves. Raw pollen percentages alone would suggest near-closed tree cover; the openness is the authors' interpretation.

Land-snail sequence from a shallow treeless valley (local signal: valley floor and slopes). Lower layers dated by Discus ruderatus and 14C (8348-8192 cal BP in layers 27-28). Open-ground species dominate from base to top, steppe snails Chondrula tridens and Helicopsis striata abundant and continuous, shade-forest species almost absent; Fruticicola fruticum peak in layers 23-29 indicates 'park-like environment with islands of trees and shrubs'. Pokorný et al. 2015 (Czech companion paper read in full).

Between the dated layers (8348-8192 and 6176-5917 cal BP): 'unusually monotonous' sequence, open-ground and semi-open species (Vallonia, Fruticicola) throughout, steppe species continuous; authors take it as proof of Holocene continuity of open dry habitats in the lower Ohře region. Local (valley-scale) evidence.

REVEALS land-cover estimate for a 25 km radius (hex-scale), early Holocene 10000-6500 BC: open land ~27% (up to 30%, falling to 15% at the end), Pinus 40-60% and Betula 10-20% of trees, Corylus to ~20% late. Authors: 'open pine-birch forests'; grasslands and open woodlands 'probably maintained by local arid climatic conditions'. Chronology: Bacon model, 9830±60 BP (9446-9211 cal BC) at 280 cm, 9410±40 BP at 252 cm; early Holocene age-depth is uncertain. Implied tree cover (complement, not stated by the paper) ~70-85%, above the 20-50% forest-steppe band.

REVEALS 25 km radius, start of the middle Holocene (6500-3000 BC): open land 12.5%, 'the maximum recorded proportion of forested land'; forests mostly coniferous, Pinus dominant with Picea to ~20% and abundant Corylus. Few Holocene 14C dates (8000-1 BC is poorly constrained).

REVEALS 25 km radius, middle Holocene 6500-3000 BC: 'the ratio of open land remained high at ca. 20%'; 'forests were mostly coniferous with dominant pine and spruce', Corylus abundant. Authors: 'Neolithic people spread into a landscape that was already open'; detectable human transformation only after 2000 BC. Note the paper is internally inconsistent on whether mid-Holocene openness was lower than early Holocene. Dated level 4715±35 BP (3632-3375 cal BC) at 185 cm.
